entry.title: CaPtain: post-training a 4B model into a code-as-policy robot agent

link.title: CaPtain: post-training a 4B model into a code-as-policy robot agent

entry.content:
Yijia Fan, Xilin He, Yilei Jiang, Dongming Wu, Jiaxu Wang, Xiangyu Yue · MMLab, CUHK · project page

Code-as-policy (CaP) agents control a robot by writing programs against perception and motion APIs. Because the program is written at test time, the agent can reuse the reasoning of a language model on tasks and scenes it was never trained for. The catch is that every strong CaP agent today runs on a closed frontier model. You cannot fine-tune it, you cannot run it on the robot, and it is not obvious how to get a small open model to the same place: an off-the-shelf 4B model placed in a CaP harness solves essentially nothing.

This post describes CaPtain, the pipeline we use to post-train Qwen3.5-4B into a working CaP agent, and the things we learned along the way. The pipeline has three parts:

  • CaPtain-Harness: a Python sandbox that exposes 22 low-level primitives (perception, geometric measurement, IK-level motion) and no high-level skills, with a text receipt for every call.
  • SFT on synthetic agent trajectories collected in that harness (generated with GPT-6 Astra), as a cold start.
  • RL with a simulator critic: a small critic reads the simulator's physical state, and the change in its predicted success across each request becomes that request's credit. The policy itself never reads this state.

Results

  • Held-out LIBERO (official initial states 11–16, 240 episodes): 55.4% → 73.8% from SFT to RL. The base model scores 0.
  • The gain persists under perturbation: +19.0 points on LIBERO-PRO Pos+Task, +17.6 on LIBERO-Plus, +21.2 and +18.8 on LIBERO-MAX Dynamic and Base.
  • On LIBERO-PRO Pos+Task the RL model, CaPtain-4B, reaches 78.5 (six-cell average), the best result we know of among systems that use neither a frontier model nor a LIBERO-trained VLA at test time.
  • Trained only on LIBERO, it runs on RoboTwin 2.0 (22.6% under the official Hard protocol), SimplerEnv (83.3% on WidowX), RoboDojo and CaP-Bench (75.0 on Cube Lift and Stack, above Gemini-3-Pro in CaP-X's multi-turn setting) without further training, and, after adaptation in a coarse simulation of the arm, on a real XR1 robot.

We report two numbers throughout. Host success is the benchmark's predicate, evaluated by the environment host on the final state. Strict success additionally requires that the agent ended the episode itself by calling finish(). Strict success is the one that matters on a robot: an agent that never says it is done cannot be deployed. RL moves both, and, as we will see below, it is the strict number that eventually breaks if you train for too long.

What the agent does

An episode is a ReAct loop of at most 60 requests. At each request the policy sees the instruction, the receipts so far and up to four camera images, and it writes one Python cell. The cell runs in a persistent session, so variables survive across requests. A typical piece of a successful episode looks like this (verbatim code, receipts shortened):

# request 6 (after the grasp): lift, re-observe, re-identify bowl and plate, measure
lift = go(np.array(obs2["value"]["robot_state"]["end_effector_position_m"]) + [0, 0, .12], q,
          speed=0.035, mode="manipulation")
obs3 = robot.observe()
b2 = robot.mark_point(obs3["value"]["observation_handle"], "agentview", .75, .421, label="held black bowl")
p2 = robot.mark_point(obs3["value"]["observation_handle"], "agentview", .78, .725, label="plate")
g2 = robot.measure_object_geometry(b2["value"]["detection_id"], p2["value"]["detection_id"])
>>> go: True none bounded Cartesian sweep reached its endpoint

# request 7: carry the bowl by the measured object-to-destination offset
transfer = np.array(obs3["value"]["robot_state"]["end_effector_position_m"])
transfer[:2] -= np.array(g2["value"]["object_to_destination_xy_offset_m"])
trans = go(transfer, q, mode="manipulation")
>>> move_to: ok; stopped_reason=target_reached executed_distance_m=0.1681 max_observed_force_n=5.198

# request 13: fresh final measurement, then finish
>>> {'object_to_destination_xy_offset_m': [0.0012, 0.0170], 'xy_distance_m': 0.0171, ...}
"The bowl is resting on the plate. Fresh measurements show a center offset of about 1.7 cm,
 within the required 2 cm tolerance."  -> robot.finish(...)

Three things in this excerpt are typical of the RL policy. It grounds objects by clicking pixels (mark_point) and back-projecting them through depth, rather than asking a text segmenter. When the bowl in the gripper hides the plate from the head camera, it switches to the wrist camera. And it checks the final relation with a fresh measurement before it calls finish().

The design of CaPtain

Low-level primitives, and receipts for everything

The harness exposes 22 capabilities in four groups: perceive (observe, segment, point, mark_point, track_target), measure (object geometry, contact geometry, comparisons of observations), act (move_to, hold, recover, release) and check (motion previews, robot state). There is no grasp(), no place(), no open_drawer() and no VLA. A grasp is something the policy has to compose: measure the object, pick an approach, descend under a force guard, close, and verify.

We made this choice deliberately. High-level skills make a benchmark easier, but they move the hard part of the problem out of the policy and into hand-written code that has to be rewritten for every robot. With low-level primitives the same API runs on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, CaP-Bench and a real robot; what changes between them is the backend below the API.

The second design choice is the receipt. Robot calls do not raise exceptions; each returns a structured result with a success flag, a failure category, a message and values, e.g. "stopped: contact · moved 0.12 m · peak 6.2 N · jaw 8 → 1 cm". A small model cannot recover from a failure it cannot see, and much of what RL improves later is how the policy reacts to these receipts.

Long episodes do not fit into the context, so when the history approaches the limit the harness compacts it turn by turn: it keeps the task context and the most recent turns verbatim, and replaces older turns with a short notice that lists the commands they ran and warns that the scene may have changed since. Because the agent's variables live in the Python session rather than in the prompt, detections, poses and helper functions survive compaction. Compaction behaves identically during RL rollouts and at test time, so the policy is trained on the inputs it will see.

Cold start, and keeping the model looking at the image

A small open model fails zero-shot in this harness, so RL has nothing to reinforce. We start with SFT on synthetic agent trajectories collected in the same harness, with the same API, task file and chat template the 4B policy uses at test time. Only assistant turns are supervised.

The most important lesson of this stage was about diversity. In an early version of our data, most episodes started from the official LIBERO initial states, where each object sits in nearly the same place across episodes (the per-object position standard deviation is about 1.4 cm). Models fine-tuned on these data looked fine on held-out states and were quietly broken: they reproduced pixel coordinates from the task identity instead of reading them from the image. Replacing the input image with a different scene left the likelihood of the predicted coordinates unchanged. The model had memorised the layouts and lost the visual grounding of the base model.

The fix was in the data, not the model. We collect SFT data on wide-layout start states (per-object standard deviation about 15 cm), mix all task suites, and randomise lighting, camera pose and materials during RL. We also mask earlier mark_point coordinates in the history with probability 0.2, so that new calls have to be grounded in the current image. With this, every mark_point and segment call is grounded in the current image, which is also what lets the policy work on the real robot later.

Credit assignment with a simulator critic

After SFT, the hard part is credit assignment. A LIBERO episode has 20–60 requests and one binary outcome at the end. Most requests only look at the scene or measure something; a handful decide the outcome. A sparse outcome reward spreads the same signal over all of them.

The observation behind CaPtain is that the simulator already knows what the policy has to infer: every object pose, whether something is in the gripper, and how many sub-goals are satisfied. We compute 36 such features \(x(s_t)\) from a hidden snapshot recorded before each request, and train a small critic on them: an ensemble of five MLPs that predicts the probability of host success from the physical state, the request index \(t\) and the task. The credit for request \(t\) is the change in that prediction:

\[\delta_t \;=\; c_t \;+\; V_\phi(s_{t+1},\,t) \;-\; V_\phi(s_t,\,t), \qquad \delta_T \;=\; c_T + R - V_\phi(s_T,\,T),\]

accumulated with GAE (\(\lambda = 0.9\), no discount), plus a group-relative outcome term over the \(G = 4\) rollouts of each start state. \(c_t \le 0\) are small costs for wasted or failed actions, and \(R\) is the terminal return.

Two details matter. First, both values in the difference use the same request index \(t\). The critic needs \(t\) to be calibrated (a half-done task at request 55 is worse than at request 5), but if the index advanced inside the difference, the passage of time alone would produce credit. Holding it fixed means the differences no longer telescope exactly, so we make no policy-invariance claim; in practice it is what keeps credit off requests that only look.

Second, the critic reads only physics. In offline studies, adding counters of the policy's own calls (how many perception calls, how many failures) made the critic slightly more accurate before the grasp, but those counters act as clocks and pulled credit onto perception requests. The same happened with the policy's LM hidden states: they decode the request index with \(R^2 = 0.80\), and used as critic inputs they moved 35% of the advantage mass onto perception requests. So the critic sees the world, not the policy.

Physical state only changes through physical actions, so the one-step term is near zero for a request that only perceives, however many tokens it produces. That request still gets credit through GAE from the action it enables. In our offline study on a 9B policy (15k episodes, 573k request states), the critic predicts final success with AUC 0.970 (0.904 within groups that share a start state). Successful grasps receive \(\Delta V = +0.058\) on average, failed grasps \(-0.0075\), and perception-only requests \(-0.0002\). 65% of the advantage mass goes to moves, 14% to grasps, 14% to releases and 1.3% to perception.

The critic is warm-started on 1,000 episodes of an earlier policy and then co-trained online, as in SAO [9]: after each round of 256 episodes it takes two steps of binary cross-entropy against host success, and each round's advantages use the critic from before that update. The policy update itself follows SAO's single-pass streaming RL with double-sided token masking (a token is kept only if \(0.2 < \pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{rollout}} < 4\)) and a small k3 KL penalty to the SFT model. At test time the critic is gone and the policy only has the harness.

Making the update move in a direction

Our first RL runs did not learn, although the pipeline itself was correct. What gave it away was that consecutive updates were nearly orthogonal. The weights were doing a random walk, with displacement growing like the square root of the number of steps.

The cause was batch size. We measured the simple gradient-noise scale \(B_{\text{noise}}\) of the 4B policy at an early checkpoint: about 9,500 episodes (95% lower bound 3,300). An update from 256 episodes is mostly noise. Accumulating gradients over \(K = 4\) rounds, i.e. 1,024 episodes per optimizer step, fixed it. The critic also helps here: on SFT rollouts of the 9B policy, per-request critic advantages (\(\lambda = 0.9\)) have a noise scale of 6.7k episodes versus 9.0k for GRPO. If we had to give one piece of advice for RL on multi-turn agents, it would be to measure \(B_{\text{noise}}\) before choosing a batch size.

Knowing when to stop

Late in training, host and strict success come apart. After about round 340, host success holds at about 65% on our monitoring stream while strict success falls from about 60% to 44%. The policy still solves the task; it just stops saying so. The lost episodes run out of requests while the agent re-measures, re-observes and re-compares a scene that is already solved.

The return structure explains why this is a slow drift rather than a cliff. A missed finish still earns 0.25, the post-success cost is capped, and the critic, trained on host success, assigns \(V \approx 1\) to every post-success state, so the decision to stop gets no credit from it at all. Only the terminal return and a small cost per request after success distinguish stopping from continuing. Because strict success drops between rounds 300 and 400, we use the round-300 checkpoint as CaPtain-4B. The cleaner fix, which we have not done yet, is to give the decision to finish its own target, for example success-and-finished.

Transfer

We evaluate CaPtain-4B, trained only on LIBERO, on three other benchmarks without further training.

  • RoboTwin 2.0 (official Hard protocol, 100 randomized trials on each of 50 tasks, run with Franka arms): 22.6% on all tasks and 30.0% on the 33 single-arm tasks, above X-VLA (20.9%) and Xiaomi-Robotics-0 (18.2%), which are trained on RoboTwin demonstrations.
  • SimplerEnv (four WidowX tasks, a new embodiment): 83.3% on average, close to ManiAgent with GPT-5 (86.8) and above PhysBrain 1.0 (80.2) and π0.5 (57.1), which are fine-tuned on Bridge data.
  • RoboDojo (42 tasks, two 6-DoF ARX X5 arms, a new embodiment): a leaderboard Score of 1.7. This is between the RoboDojo team's agent driven by GPT-5.5 (1.1) and by DeepSeek-Flash (3.0), and above RDT (0.5) and OpenVLA-OFT (0.2) trained on RoboDojo's own data; GPT-6 Astra reaches 29.0. The most frequent failure is reach: the top-down workspace of the X5 ends about 0.5 m from its base.
  • CaP-Bench (Cube Lift and Cube Stack at CaP-Gym's step horizon): 75.0, above CaP-X's multi-turn visual agents on Gemini-3-Pro (73.5), GPT-5.2 (55.5) and Claude Opus 4.5 (54.0), and above a 7B coder trained with RL on these tasks (62.0).

RoboDojo is where the limits show. Tasks that need two arms at the same time, handovers or memory remain unsolved; the policy acts with one arm at a time. These are the next targets for the critic: it values a grasp because the simulator can see the grasp, and there is no reason it could not value coordination or termination in the same way.

A real robot

The same harness runs on an XR1 arm with a head RGB-D camera and a wrist camera; the simulator is replaced by a hardware backend with a kinematic twin and safety guards, and the policy-facing API and receipts are unchanged. The XR1 differs from the simulated Panda in kinematics, reach, gripper geometry and camera placement, so we use a checkpoint fine-tuned on episodes from a coarse simulation of the XR1, built from primitive objects and untextured surfaces. The policy is adapted with simulated XR1 episodes only and uses no real-world data.

Both tasks are completed with the same low-level primitives used in simulation. In the second, the instruction names neither object, so the agent resolves the references from the image before it acts: the pale-blue cube matches the sky, and of the two containers the white bowl is round, so the tray is the target.

Open questions

  • Stopping. Termination should get its own credit target; host success is the wrong label for the decision to finish.
  • Two arms. The harness supports both arms, but the policy rarely coordinates them. A critic over joint two-arm state is the obvious next step.
  • Privileged state off the simulator. The critic needs object poses that a real robot does not have. In our offline study, a critic fed estimated poses agrees less with the simulator critic (correlation 0.49 with 2 cm pose noise, 0.36 with 5 cm), so RL on hardware needs a better state estimate than we have today.
  • More than one training benchmark. RL used only the 40 LIBERO tasks. We do not yet know how far the gains transfer when RL itself sees more embodiments.

Release

We release CaPtain-Harness, the training code, the SFT data and the CaPtain-4B weights (links on the project page; the paper will follow on arXiv).
